notes: Marker: first-person pronoun 僕 (boku), used by male speakers; standard masculine self-reference in the polite register.
Marker: first-person pronoun 俺 (ore), strongly masculine, reinforced by the masculine sentence-final particle ぜ (ze). Rough casual male speech.
Marker: possessive 俺の (ore no); 俺 is a strongly masculine first-person pronoun.
Marker: sentence-final particle ぜ (ze), strongly masculine casual particle (a register particle rather than a politeness particle; tagged with the closest sentence-final-particle tag).
Markers: first-person pronoun あたし (atashi, feminine) plus sentence-final particle わ (wa, feminine with rising intonation). Stereotypically feminine speech style.

text: あたしはコーヒーが好き。
notes: Marker: first-person pronoun あたし (atashi), used by female speakers in casual speech.

glossEn: I wonder if it will rain tomorrow.
notes: Marker: sentence-final particle かしら (kashira, 'I wonder'), chiefly used by female speakers in modern standard Japanese.
Marker: sentence-final combination わよ (wa yo), assertive feminine particle. 私 itself is neutral — the gender signal is わよ.
私 (watashi) is gender-neutral in the polite register and no other marker is present. (In plain casual speech watashi can lean feminine, but with です it is the default neutral pronoun.)

glossEn: I will get up early tomorrow.
notes: First-person statement with dropped pronoun and polite ます form; no speaker-gender marker.

text: 田中さんは毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
notes: Third-person statement; さん is gender-neutral; no speaker-gender marker.

text: 今日は天気がいいですね。
glossEn: The weather is nice today, isn't it?
notes: Impersonal statement; sentence-final ね is gender-neutral.

text: 弟は「俺は行くぜ」と言いました。
notes: 俺 and ぜ sit inside the quotation and mark the quoted speaker (the brother), not the narrator; the matrix sentence carries no speaker-gender marker.
兄 (my older brother) genders the referent only; Japanese kinship terms are used by speakers of any gender (unlike Korean 형/오빠).
